title: Domain Dependence
hook: The rule works perfectly in one room, then disappears the moment the setting changes.
counterintuition: Knowing a principle does not mean it will travel; the safer move is to name the new context, translate the rule, and make the transfer visible before deciding.
tryThisNow: Take one rule you use well at work. Write how that same rule should change one home, money, health, or travel choice.
keyTakeaway: Do not trust a principle to transfer by itself. Translate it into the new context before you act.

breakdown.fastRead: A hotel desk uses fairness well for room upgrades, then forgets the same rule when families are overbooked after midnight. The rule did not fail. The transfer failed. Domain dependence appears when a lesson stays trapped where you learned it. A rule for one setting does not travel by itself. Name the new setting, translate the rule, and make the next action show the transfer.
breakdown.deepRead:
A manager is careful with risk at work and reckless with holiday spending at home. A nurse follows checklists on the ward and guesses when booking her own travel insurance. A farmer understands weather uncertainty in the field and treats a building plan as if forecasts were promises. The mind knows the rule somewhere, but not everywhere.

Domain dependence means judgment can be tied to its setting. You may understand incentives in finance but miss them in family decisions. You may understand base rates in medicine but ignore them in hiring. You may understand safety buffers at work but forget them in a rental-car queue. The principle is available, yet the context fails to call it up.

Knowledge often wears a location tag.

The correction is active transfer. Do not ask, 'Do I know this idea?' Ask, 'Where else should this idea apply right now?' Then translate the rule into the new setting. If incentives distort workers in a factory, they can distort children, clients, donors, and drivers. If averages hide risk in weather, they can hide risk in staffing, rent, and scheduling. The words may change, but the structure travels.

This matters because intelligence can become strangely local. People look wise in the domain that trained them and naive in the neighboring domain that uses the same pattern. The fix is not to memorize more principles. It is to build a small bridge at the moment of choice: same pattern, new setting, visible action.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hotel overbooking desk has a visitor badge from a corporate guest and a lobby full of tired families. The desk manager knows how to apply fairness rules to loyalty upgrades. She can explain priority order, documented need, and compensation. At 11:40 p.m., with three rooms short, she is about to protect the corporate guest and scatter the families because the upgrade rule feels like hotel policy while the family rule feels like improvisation. The same fairness principle is available. It has not crossed the border.

Domain dependence is the failure of transfer. A person may have a sound principle, but the principle stays bound to the domain where it was learned. It behaves like a tool stored in the wrong building. You can own it and still not have it in your hand when the context changes.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb's aphorism about the businessman in Dubai captures the absurd version: a porter carries the man's luggage at the hotel, then the same man lifts free weights in the gym. Strength is valued in one domain and outsourced in another. A study title such as 'Interspousal aggression in law enforcement families: A preliminary investigation' points toward a darker version of the same problem: training, authority, or control in one official setting does not guarantee wise conduct in a private one. Skills do not automatically migrate.

Where do you become strangely stupid because the room changed?

A chemicals plant sees the same pattern in incentives. The safety team understands that bonuses can distort behavior on the production line, yet the review committee is about to reward managers for low reported incidents without checking near-miss logs. The principle is already known: incentives shape reporting. The context shift hides it. The transfer move is to write 'same incentive problem' on the sample tray, add near-misses to the metric, and refuse to let the new domain erase the old lesson.

The limit matters. Not every principle transfers cleanly. A rule that works in farming may fail in pediatric appointments because people, timing, and ethics differ. A hotel rule may not fit a ferry fog-delay rule without adaptation. Transfer is not copy-paste. It is translation. Ask which part of the pattern is structural and which part is local. Then change the wording until the principle fits the new terrain.

The practical move is to keep a small transfer checklist. What is the principle? Where did I learn it? What is the new domain? What would the same pattern look like here? What action would prove I applied it? This checklist catches the moment when you know the right idea but fail to summon it because the setting is different.

The best evidence of transfer is behavior. Mark the visitor badge and change the overbooking order. Mark the sample tray and change the incentive metric. Mark the weather log and change the car-rental insurance script. A principle has not transferred until the next choice looks different.

Annette, the night manager, must decide whether to protect the corporate guest or reapply the fairness rule she uses for upgrades. She writes domain dependence on the badge, translates the rule to family displacement, and changes the room order while the clerk updates compensation.

examples.whyItMatters: A principle can stay trapped in the policy area where it is familiar.

examples.title: The safety bonus that forgets reporting incentives

Cyril must decide whether to approve the incentive or transfer the reporting lesson from production audits. He marks transfer on the tray, adds near-miss reports to the metric, and changes the bonus formula in front of the safety lead.

examples.title: The appointment default that ignores no-shows
examples.scenario: The inspection tag clicks against Brenda's clipboard as she stands beside the pediatric clinic's stroller row. She must decide whether to copy the hospital's adult appointment default or translate it for parents juggling school pickups. She circles context on the tag, adds a text-confirm step for late afternoon slots, and changes the schedule before the receptionist prints reminders.

examples.title: The rainfall forecast that forgets uncertainty
examples.scenario: You are looking at a floor plan in a Nebraska farm office while the rainfall projection is still open on the laptop. Ronald must decide whether to build storage from the average forecast or transfer the uncertainty rule he uses in planting. He writes principle on the floor plan, adds a dry-year storage margin, and changes the bid before the contractor prices the slab.
examples.whatToDo: Carry the weather-uncertainty principle from planting into the building decision.
examples.whyItMatters: A farmer can respect forecast limits in one domain and forget them in another.

examples.title: The rental counter that forgets tail risk
examples.scenario: It took Jill two winter claims in Calgary to see that customers understood risk at the ski hill but forgot it at the car-rental counter. The weather log showed black-ice days, yet the insurance script treated drivers like ordinary tourists. She must decide whether to keep the upsell script. She writes blind spot on the log, translates the slope-risk language to roads, and changes the script before the next storm weekend.
examples.whatToDo: Use the risk language customers already understand in the domain where they need it now.
examples.whyItMatters: People can grasp danger in one context and miss the same structure at a counter.

examples.title: The ferry rule borrowed from sport scoring
examples.scenario: What does a score sheet know about ferry fog? Carl, the operations lead, places one beside the 2:30 p.m. Maine ferry postmortem after a morning of angry delay calls. The port already scores storm risk for inspections, but fog delays are handled by habit. He writes domain on the sheet, transfers the scoring rule to visibility and tide, and changes the delay threshold while the captain reviews the log.
examples.whatToDo: Move a risk-scoring principle from one maritime domain into the fog-delay rule.
examples.whyItMatters: A useful domain rule can sit nearby while a neighboring decision runs on instinct.

reviewCards.front: You know a rule in one setting but miss it elsewhere. How should the rule transfer contexts?
reviewCards.back: Translate the rule into the new setting before acting. Knowledge in one domain does not move itself across contexts.
Ask where else this same pattern applies right now, then translate the principle into the new setting.
The structure may travel, but the local constraints change. Transfer means translation, not blind copying.

reviewCards.front: What proves a principle has transferred?
reviewCards.back: A visible action changes in the new domain: a metric, rule, script, reserve, threshold, or default.
Say, 'Same pattern, new setting,' then write the version of the rule that fits the current choice.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Make transfer explicit by naming the old domain, the new domain, and the concrete action that carries the principle across.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I use a principle well at work, then I will write its home version before a personal decision.
If a rule worked elsewhere, then I will translate it for the local context before copying it.
If I recognize a risk pattern in one domain, then I will ask where the same structure appears nearby.
If someone says this situation is different, then I will ask which part is different and which pattern is the same.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one principle you apply in one domain. Write its version for a current decision in another domain and change one action to match.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a mistake and ask which principle you knew elsewhere but failed to transfer.

memorableLines.text: Knowledge often wears a location tag.
A principle has not transferred until the next choice looks different.
